newsitem.title: UK: Lift beef ban or UK MPs will oppose cow cull - Hogg.
newsitem.headline: Lift beef ban or UK MPs will oppose cow cull - Hogg.

text.p: British Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg admitted on Wednesday there would be a "huge degree" of parliamentary opposition to approving a selective cull of cattle most at risk of mad cow disease unless the European Union agreed "rapidly and substantially" to lift a ban on British beef sales.

"The House of Commons will want to know whether in return for a cull policy we, the government, expect the European Union member states rapidly and substantially to lift the ban in accordance with the Florence criteria," Hogg told reporters.

"I think that that lies absolutely at the heart of the problem that we face. If the House of Commons can be told, and believes, that Europe would rapidly and substantially lift the ban, then I think the House of Commons would be willing to approve a cull. If, on the contrary, they cannot be reassured on that point, then I think there would be a huge degree of parliamentary opposition to the cull policy," Hogg added.
Asked whether Britain was not committed to a selective cull under the terms of a deal struck with its EU partners at the Florence summit in June, Hogg said:

"What was agreed at Florence was a process whereby we would see scientific and objective criteria applied and which would bring about a rapid and substantial lifting of the ban. That is what everybody contemplated."

Hogg was speaking a day after EU farm ministers rejected Britain's bid to reduce the slaughter of up to 147,000 cattle in light of a report by scientists from Oxford University showing Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), or mad cow disease, would die out within five years even without a cull.
Newspapers have speculated that Britain will tear up the Florence agreement. Prime Minister John Major said earlier on Wednesday no decision had been taken.

Hogg said: "I have to be able to go the House of Commons, if I'm going to seek authority for a cull, and say that in my considered view member states are likely rapidly and substantially to lift the ban.
"If I can do that honestly, then I think that there would be a reasonable prospect of the House of Commons being prepared to authorise a cull -- and if not, I fancy not."
